title: Saul Didn't Begin as a Villain
paragraphs:
Saul Didn't Begin as a Villain
The Most Feared Enemy of the Church Wasn't Born Evil—He Was Convinced He Was Serving God. That Should Terrify Every One of Us.
There is something deeply unsettling about Saul of Tarsus.
Not because he persecuted Christians.
Not because he approved of Stephen's execution.
Not because he dragged believers from their homes, separating families and filling prisons.
Those things are horrifying enough.
But the most terrifying truth about Saul is this:
He believed he was right.
That is what makes his story so unforgettable.

History remembers villains who knowingly embrace evil. Scripture gives us something far more sobering—a man who loved God, studied Scripture, prayed, fasted, defended truth, and yet found himself fighting against the very Messiah he claimed to be waiting for.
That should humble every Christian.
Because if it happened to Saul, we should never assume we are beyond self-deception.
Saul was not introduced in Scripture as a monster.
He was introduced as a brilliant young Pharisee.
Educated.
Disciplined.
Respected.
Passionate.
Absolutely convinced that he was protecting the holiness of Israel.
When Stephen preached that Jesus of Nazareth was the promised Messiah, Saul did not hear hope.
He heard blasphemy.
Acts tells us that those who stoned Stephen laid their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul (Acts 7:58), and immediately afterward Scripture records something chilling:
"And Saul approved of his execution." (Acts 8:1)
Those few words reveal a heart completely persuaded that violence against Christians honored God.
Imagine that.
He wasn't chasing pleasure.
He wasn't driven by greed.
He wasn't building an empire.
He sincerely believed he was defending the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
That is exactly why Jesus later asked him one of the most penetrating questions ever spoken.
Not...
"Why are you persecuting Christians?"
Not...
"Why are you hurting innocent people?"
Instead He said,
"Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?" (Acts 9:4)
Because Jesus is so united with His people that every wound inflicted upon His Church is felt personally by Christ Himself.
That truth alone should change how we treat one another.
Saul's confidence came from years of religious excellence.
He later described himself this way:
"Circumcised the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee... as to righteousness under the law, blameless." (Philippians 3:5–6)
Notice something remarkable.
He never claimed to have been lazy.
He wasn't spiritually indifferent.
He wasn't morally reckless.
He was extraordinarily devoted.
Yet devotion without Christ still leaves a person spiritually blind.
That is one of the central messages of the Gospel.
Religion alone cannot save.
Only Jesus can.

Saul's very name reflects his Jewish identity. In Hebrew it is שָׁאוּל (Sha'ul), meaning "asked for" or "requested," the same name as Israel's first king. His Roman name, Paul (Paulos in Greek, Παῦλος), simply means "small" or "humble." Scripture never says Jesus renamed him. Rather, Acts gradually begins using his Roman name as his ministry increasingly focused on the Gentile world (Acts 13:9). This detail reminds us that the transformation was not in his name but in his heart.
His story reached its turning point on the road to Damascus.
He traveled there carrying official authority to arrest followers of Jesus.
His destination was destruction.
But heaven had another plan.
Luke records:
"Suddenly a light from heaven shone around him." (Acts 9:3)

The Greek word translated "light" is φῶς (phōs), meaning light, radiance, or divine illumination. Throughout the New Testament, phōs often symbolizes God's self-revelation, exposing darkness and revealing truth (John 1:4–9). Saul was not merely startled by brightness; he was confronted by the glory of the risen Christ.
Then came the voice.
"Σαούλ, Σαούλ, τί με διώκεις;" (Saoul, Saoul, ti me diōkeis?)
Translated literally:
"Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?"
The Greek verb διώκω (diōkō) means to pursue, chase down, persecute, or relentlessly hunt. Saul thought he was pursuing heretics. In reality, he was pursuing the Lord Himself.
The response is heartbreaking.
"Who are You, Lord?"
Not because Saul lacked intelligence.
Because everything he thought he knew suddenly collapsed.
Then came the answer that changed history forever.
"I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting."
One sentence.
One revelation.
One encounter.
Everything changed.
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not begin with condemnation.
He did not immediately recite every sin Saul had committed.
He first revealed Himself.
Because true repentance begins when we see Christ as He truly is.
The Hebrew Scriptures had long anticipated this reality. In Isaiah 53:5 we read:
וְהוּא מְחֹלָל מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ (Vehu mecholal mippesha'einu)
"He was pierced because of our transgressions."

The Servant whom Israel awaited had indeed come—not as a political conqueror, but as the suffering Messiah who bore humanity's sin. Saul knew Isaiah. Yet until he encountered Jesus, he had not understood that the prophecy pointed to Him.
Grace often arrives where judgment seems most deserved.
Saul deserved justice.
Instead, he received mercy.
The man who hunted Christians became one.
The man who imprisoned believers wrote letters that now strengthen believers around the world.
The man who tried to silence the Gospel became its greatest missionary.
Only Jesus writes stories like that.
Some people wonder whether Saul's conversion was too dramatic to be believable.
Yet that is precisely the point.
The Gospel is not merely about improving people.
It is about making them new.
As Paul later wrote:
"Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come." (2 Corinthians 5:17)
The Greek phrase καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis) means "a new creation"—not merely repaired or upgraded, but something qualitatively new. The Gospel does not simply polish a life; it recreates it.
Perhaps the most beautiful irony in Saul's story is found in the meaning of the Gospel itself.
The Greek word εὐαγγέλιον (euangelion) means "good news."
Not good advice.
Not self-improvement.
Not religious achievement.
Good news.
News announces what has already been accomplished.
Jesus accomplished what sinners never could.
That is why salvation is by grace through faith (Ephesians 2:8–9), not by works, lest anyone should boast.

Saul spent years believing righteousness could be attained through strict observance of the Law. After meeting Christ, he understood that the Law reveals sin but cannot justify the sinner (Romans 3:20). Justification comes through faith in Jesus Christ, who fulfilled the Law perfectly and bore its curse on our behalf (Galatians 3:13).
Perhaps this is where Saul's story intersects with yours.
Maybe you have never arrested Christians.
Maybe you have never breathed threats against the Church.
But have you ever mistaken religious activity for a relationship with Christ?
Have you ever defended traditions while neglecting love?
Have you ever assumed that because you know about God, you truly know Him?
Saul reminds us that sincerity is not enough.
Truth matters.
And truth is ultimately found in a Person.
Jesus said,
"I am the way, and the truth, and the life." (John 14:6)
Notice He did not merely teach truth.
He is Truth.

If you have wandered, the same Savior who met Saul on the Damascus road still calls sinners to Himself today. His grace is not reserved for those with spotless records. It is extended to all who repent and believe the Gospel. No past is beyond His redemption, and no heart is too hardened for His transforming power.
If this story has exposed something hidden in your own heart, don't keep it there. Be honest before God. Your words may encourage another person who is quietly wrestling with the same questions.

Your support helps us create Christ-centered articles, devotionals, discipleship resources, and Gospel content that reaches more people with the hope of Jesus. More importantly, your partnership is an act of stewardship that helps advance Gospel-centered ministry.
Because in the end, Saul's story was never really about Saul.
It has always been about Jesus.
The Savior who turns persecutors into preachers.
The Redeemer who transforms enemies into family.
The King who replaces shame with purpose.
The Shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to pursue the one.
The Author who still takes lives that seem ruined beyond repair and writes endings no human could ever imagine.
Scandal is never the final chapter when Christ holds the pen.
